source.title: The Debt Trap
source.summary: From Ottoman debt to IMF programs: how sovereign lending creates dependency, and where borrowers share responsibility.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: In 1881, European creditors established the Ottoman Public Debt Administration, taking control of Ottoman state revenues. A century later, the IMF offered structural adjustment programs to dozens of countries including many Muslim-majority nations. The pattern has similarities, but the reality is more nuanced than simple predation. IMF loans come at below-market rates, and countries like South Korea used them as a bridge to reform. Others, like Pakistan, cycled through program after program without making structural changes, a failure of domestic governance as much as external pressure. This episode traces the evolution of sovereign lending, examines what structural adjustment actually did in Egypt, Pakistan, Indonesia, and Nigeria, and asks harder questions about shared responsibility between lenders and borrowers.

thread: The Ottoman Empire lost control of its own tax revenues to European creditors in 1881. The IMF structural adjustment programs are the modern version of the same arrangement.
South Korea used IMF loans as a bridge to reform and transformed its economy. Pakistan has cycled through program after program for decades without structural change.
The pattern repeats because sovereign lending creates dependency by design. Creditors get control over state revenues and policy. Borrowers surrender sovereignty for liquidity.

Egypt, Pakistan, Indonesia, Nigeria all followed the same script. The question isn't whether the trap exists but why some countries escape while others remain caught. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-be-2

linkedin.post: The Ottoman Public Debt Administration of 1881 was a turning point in sovereign finance. European creditors took direct control of Ottoman state revenues after the empire defaulted on its debts. A century later, the IMF offered structural adjustment programs to dozens of countries, including many Muslim-majority nations. The mechanics are different, but the pattern is remarkably similar: surrender policy autonomy for financial assistance. What's striking is how outcomes varied. South Korea used IMF programs as a bridge to economic transformation. Pakistan has cycled through program after program without making fundamental reforms. The difference often comes down to domestic governance and political will. The debt trap is real, but it's not just about predatory lending. It's about the choices borrowing nations make when they have room to maneuver. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-be-2
